title: The crater of Vesuvius from Naples: how to get up, the timed ticket and the walk to the rim
subtitle: A train and a shuttle, or one bus from the city, then a ticket for a fixed hour and half an hour on foot.
excerpt: How to reach the crater of Vesuvius from Naples: by train to Ercolano or Pompeii and a shuttle, or by bus from the city. How the timed entry works, what the walk to the rim is like, and what each of the partner's listings includes.

meta_title: Vesuvius crater from Naples: how to get up
meta_description: Train to Ercolano or Pompeii and a shuttle, or a bus from Naples: how to reach the crater of Vesuvius, how the timed ticket works, and the walk up.

featured_image.alt: The two peaks of Vesuvius seen across the water of the Bay of Naples at sunset

content_html:
[place attraction="vesuvius-national-park" city="naples"]

In 1880 a funicular railway opened on the upper cone of Vesuvius, and to mark the occasion a journalist, Peppino Turco, and a composer, Luigi Denza, wrote a song. "Funiculì, Funiculà" outlived the railway by a long way. The line was badly damaged by the eruption of 1906, rebuilt, and destroyed for good in March 1944, when the volcano erupted for the last time to date, sent lava through the village of San Sebastiano and buried an American airfield in ash.

A chairlift took its place from 1953 and closed in 1984. Since then nothing mechanical has gone to the top. A road climbs to about 1,000 metres and the rest is on foot. That turns the visit into a small piece of planning: a way up the road, a ticket for a fixed hour, and a walk.

What you are going to see

The summit stands at 1,281 metres. The crater is roughly half a kilometre across and about 300 metres deep, with walls of grey and rust-red rock. There is no lava and no glow. On most days thin steam rises from vents in the inner wall, which is the only sign that the volcano is active. It is watched without pause by an observatory founded in 1841, the oldest of its kind in the world.

The other half of the visit is the view. On a clear day you see the whole Bay of Naples, with Capri, the Sorrento peninsula and the city. In summer there is often haze by late morning.

The inside of the crater from the rim path: rock, scree and, on most days, a little steam. Photo: Norbert Nagel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Three ways up the road

Train to Ercolano, then a shuttle

The Circumvesuviana is the commuter railway that runs round the bay. Trains towards Sorrento leave from Napoli Garibaldi, the station beneath the central station, and reach Ercolano Scavi in about twenty minutes. The shuttle office is on the square outside. This is the shortest road up, and the ruins of Herculaneum are ten minutes downhill from the same station, so the two fit in one day.

Train to Pompeii, then a shuttle

The same line continues to the stop for the ruins of Pompeii. Shuttles for the crater also leave from Pompeii, and this suits a day with the ruins in the morning and the volcano after lunch. Check the meeting point: the shuttle our partner sells starts from an office in the modern town of Pompei, by the state railway station, which is a good twenty minutes on foot from the gate of the ruins most people use.

A bus straight from Naples

Coaches and minibuses leave from the streets beside the central station and drive to the car park at the top of the road. It is the simplest way and takes about half a day, door to door. Traffic on the way out of Naples can make the bus late.

You can also drive. In recent seasons private cars have had to park lower down, with a paid shuttle or a walk along the road for the last stretch. The arrangement has changed more than once, so look it up before you set out.

The timed ticket

The crater lies inside Vesuvius National Park, and the path to the rim starts behind a gate. In recent seasons the park has sold crater tickets online only, for a fixed entry time, with no ticket desk at the gate. Phone signal up there is poor. People who arrive without a ticket have been turned back, so treat booking ahead as part of the trip and check the current rule.

When entry is bundled with a shuttle, the operator holds the ticket and matches it to the bus. The entry time is strict in one direction: you are not let in before it.

The park closes the path in strong wind, storms and thick cloud, sometimes at short notice. What happens then differs from one listing to another: a full refund, a partial one, another date, or a drive round the cone instead. Read that line before you pay.

The walk to the rim

From the gate a wide track of loose volcanic gravel climbs in long bends. It takes twenty to thirty minutes and gains less than 200 metres of height, steeply enough to notice. There are no steps and no shade, and it does not suit wheelchairs or pushchairs. At the top the path follows part of the rim behind a fence. The park's own volcanological guides stand there and give short talks, which are covered by the entry ticket.

Shuttles usually leave you about an hour and a half between drop-off and departure, which is enough for the walk up, the rim and the walk down. Wear closed shoes with a grip, because the gravel gets into sandals. Carry water and a hat, and a windproof layer: the top is several degrees colder than Naples and often windy.

On the rim: red gravel, a wooden fence and no shade. Photo: Michal Osmenda, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Entry with the shuttle from Ercolano: the park ticket and the return ride from the office by the station. The guide is the park's, at the top only.
  • Entry with a return bus from Naples: two listings from two operators, both leaving from beside the central station. Park ticket and transport, with the same guides at the top.
  • Entry with the shuttle from Pompeii: as above, from modern Pompei. There is also a sunset departure, which lists an hour and a half of free time at the crater and no guided tour.
  • Entry ticket with a guidebook: no transport. Someone meets you at the park entrance with the ticket and a booklet, and you get yourself up the mountain. The listing says it has no tickets for children under six.

"Skip the line" on these means the ticket is booked for your slot. Everyone walks the same path. Buses take small bags only, and nothing can be left on board while you are at the crater.

These are the Vesuvius tickets and transfers our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="naples" match="vesuvius" limit="6"]

When to go

Go in the morning for clearer air. In July and August the dark gravel is hot by midday. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Winter days can be very clear and very cold, and closures are more frequent. Weekends and Italian holidays fill the slots first. Opening hours change month by month: see our page for Vesuvius National Park.

Naples and its bay from the upper slopes, through the usual haze. Photo: DimiTalen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

From here

The towns the volcano buried in AD 79 lie at its foot. Pompeii needs at least half a day, and Herculaneum, in Ercolano, about two hours. The best of what was found in both is in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples, which is the place for a day when the mountain is in cloud. The attractions map of Italy shows the rest of the bay.

Cover photo: Massimo Finizio, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0 IT.

faqs.q: How do you get to the crater of Vesuvius from Naples?
faqs.a: Take the Circumvesuviana train to Ercolano Scavi or to Pompeii and a shuttle bus up the mountain, or take a bus that goes straight from the central station in Naples. The road ends at about 1,000 metres and the rest is a walk.

faqs.q: Do you need to book Vesuvius in advance?
faqs.a: Yes, plan on it. In recent seasons crater tickets have been sold online only, for a fixed entry time, with no desk at the gate. Check the current rule before you go.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to the crater of Vesuvius?
faqs.a: Twenty to thirty minutes uphill on a wide track of loose gravel, with less than 200 metres of climb. There are no steps and no shade.

faqs.q: Can you visit Vesuvius and Pompeii in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. Shuttles to the crater leave from Pompeii, so the usual plan is the ruins in the morning and the volcano in the afternoon. Check where the shuttle starts, because modern Pompei and the ruins have different stations.

faqs.q: What happens if Vesuvius is closed for bad weather?
faqs.a: The park closes the path in strong wind, storms and thick cloud. Depending on the listing you get a full refund, a partial refund or another date, so read that condition before you book.

title: Herculaneum instead of Pompeii: a half day from Naples, and how the Vesuvius combined tickets work
subtitle: A Roman town a tenth of the size, twenty minutes by train, with its upper floors and its wood still in place.
excerpt: What Herculaneum has that Pompeii does not, what to see in two hours, how to get there from Naples, whether to visit it instead of Pompeii or after it, and what the combined tickets with Vesuvius really include.
secondary_keywords: how to get to Herculaneum from Naples
longtail_phrases: is Herculaneum better than Pompeii
how long do you need at Herculaneum
how do you get from Naples to Herculaneum by train
can you do Herculaneum and Vesuvius in one day
can you see Pompeii and Herculaneum on the same day
meta_title: Herculaneum instead of Pompeii: a half day from Naples
meta_description: What Herculaneum has that Pompeii lacks, what to see in two hours, the train from Naples, and what the combined tickets with Vesuvius include.

featured_image.alt: The excavated houses of Herculaneum in their pit, with the modern town of Ercolano on the edge above

content_html:
[place attraction="house-of-the-deer-herculaneum" city="naples"]

In 1709 workmen sinking a well in the village of Resina, on the coast south of Naples, brought up pieces of fine marble from far underground. They had hit the stage of a Roman theatre. The prince who owned the land had the shaft widened and carried off the statues. From 1738 the king of Naples took over and dug on through tunnels, because the town lay under about twenty metres of volcanic material that had set like rock.

That depth explains Herculaneum. Most of it has never been dug out, since the modern town, renamed Ercolano in 1969, stands on top. What has been uncovered is better preserved than anything at Pompeii. It is also smaller and closer to Naples. So the question is a fair one: can it replace Pompeii, or is it an extra, and are the combined tickets with the volcano a sensible way to see it.

What is different from Pompeii

  • Size. Pompeii is a whole city and needs four hours at the least. The open part of Herculaneum is roughly a tenth of that: a few blocks of streets, which two hours cover.
  • Height. At Pompeii the roofs gave way under falling pumice. Here many houses stand to their upper floor, with balconies and stairs.
  • Wood. At Pompeii it rotted. Here the heat charred it and the mud sealed it: beams, doors, a folding screen, the frame of a bed, the racks of a wine shop with its jars still on them.
  • The people. For two centuries it was thought that the townspeople had escaped. Then, from 1980, some three hundred skeletons were found crowded into the arched boat sheds on the old beach, where they had waited for rescue by sea.
  • What is missing. No forum, no amphitheatre, no large temples: the public centre is still under Ercolano. Pompeii shows you how a city worked. Herculaneum shows you how people lived indoors.

Arched vaults at the seaward edge of the town, below the houses. Photo: Norbert Nagel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What to see in two hours

  • The old shore. You go down to it through the bank of volcanic rock, which is the best measure of how deep the town was buried. The sea is now several hundred metres away.
  • The House of the Deer. A rich house whose garden terrace once looked over the water, named after its marble groups of deer attacked by hounds.
  • The House of Neptune and Amphitrite. A wall mosaic in coloured glass, as bright as when it was set, and the wine shop next door.
  • The Samnite House. One of the oldest, with a tall atrium and a gallery of small columns round its upper level.
  • The House of the Wooden Partition, for the charred screen that divided its hall.
  • The baths, with separate sections for men and women and a sea-creature mosaic on the floor.
  • The College of the Augustales, a hall with wall paintings of Hercules, after whom the town was named.

Houses are closed in turn for conservation, so do not count on any single one.

The wall mosaic that gives the House of Neptune and Amphitrite its name. Photo: Justin Benttinen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Getting there from Naples

Take the Circumvesuviana, the commuter railway round the bay, from Napoli Garibaldi, beneath the central station, in the direction of Sorrento. Ercolano Scavi is about twenty minutes away. Trains are frequent, crowded and without reserved seats, and pickpockets work them. From the station walk straight down the main street for ten minutes, to the gate at the bottom.

The park sells its own entry ticket, at the gate and online. Leave Naples by nine and you are back for a late lunch.

Instead of Pompeii, or after it

  • One full day and your first Roman town: Pompeii. Nothing replaces the scale.
  • Half a day, great heat, children, or a dislike of crowds: Herculaneum instead. You will see finer houses and walk a fraction of the distance.
  • Both in one day: possible, since they are on the same railway line. Do Pompeii in the morning and stop at Herculaneum on the way back, when you are tired and it is small. Check the hour of last admission.
  • Both, comfortably: two separate half days.

They are two parks with two tickets. Entry to one does not cover the other.

The atrium of the Samnite House, with its upper gallery still standing. Photo: Carole Raddato, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

How the combined tickets with Vesuvius work

Our partner sells no plain entry ticket for Herculaneum. It sells bundles, and one audio tour:

  • Herculaneum and Vesuvius, with return transport from Naples. A minibus from beside the central station, entry to the ruins and to the crater path, and free time at each. Nobody guides you through the ruins.
  • The same pair from Pompei, starting at an office in the modern town. It suits people staying on that side of the bay. This listing states that no guide and no audio guide are included.
  • Pompeii, Herculaneum and Vesuvius in one day, from Naples or from Pompei: three entries and the transport between them, with an audio guide and a map for Pompeii only. It is a long day that leaves about two hours a site, which is right for Herculaneum and thin for Pompeii.
  • An audio tour of Herculaneum, in the partner's app on your own phone: a two-hour route through the houses. It includes no entry ticket, which you buy at the gate. Bring earphones.

What a bundle buys is mostly transport. No railway goes up the volcano, and the pairing makes sense on the map, because the shortest road to the crater starts beside the station of Ercolano. If the commuter train and a shuttle do not bother you, you can build the same day yourself. Two more things to read on the listing: what is refunded if the crater path is closed by weather, and which age group you belong to, since the park has free and reduced entry for the young.

These are the Herculaneum combinations and the audio tour our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="naples" match="herculaneum,herculan" limit="5"]

Practical notes

The Roman paving is uneven and there are steps into most houses. The site lies in a pit below the level of the town, so in summer it is hot and still by noon: go in the first two hours or the last two. Carry water. Opening hours differ between summer and winter, so check them before you travel.

From here

Up the main street towards the station, the Virtual Archaeological Museum rebuilds the town on screens, which children like after the real thing. The Villa of the Papyri, where a library of charred scrolls was found in the 1750s, lies beside the park and is not normally open. Its bronzes are in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples, with the best of the wall paintings. See what else there is in Ercolano, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Norbert Nagel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Is Herculaneum better than Pompeii?
faqs.a: It is better preserved and far smaller. Houses keep their upper floors, their mosaics and even charred wood. Pompeii gives you a whole city with its forum and amphitheatre, which Herculaneum cannot.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Herculaneum?
faqs.a: About two hours for the open part of the town. With the train from Naples and back it makes a comfortable half day.

faqs.q: How do you get from Naples to Herculaneum by train?
faqs.a: Take the Circumvesuviana from Napoli Garibaldi towards Sorrento and get off at Ercolano Scavi, about twenty minutes away. The gate is ten minutes downhill on foot.

faqs.q: Can you do Herculaneum and Vesuvius in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. The shortest road to the crater starts beside the station of Ercolano, so the two pair naturally, on your own or with a combined ticket that includes transport.

faqs.q: Can you see Pompeii and Herculaneum on the same day?
faqs.a: Yes, they are on the same railway line. See Pompeii in the morning and stop at Herculaneum on the way back to Naples. Each has its own entry ticket.

title: Palermo and Monreale: what is free, what needs a ticket, and how to get up to Monreale
subtitle: Two Norman cathedrals, a cloister with its own door, two museums, and a bus up the hill.
excerpt: What you can see for nothing in Palermo and at Monreale, which doors have a ticket desk behind them (the cloister of Monreale, the Salinas museum, Palazzo Riso), how to reach Monreale, and what the partner's tickets include.
secondary_keywords: how to get to Monreale from Palermo
longtail_phrases: is Monreale Cathedral free to enter
is the cloister of Monreale worth it
how do you get from Palermo to Monreale by bus
is Palermo Cathedral free
what is in the Salinas museum in Palermo
meta_title: Palermo and Monreale: what is free, what needs a ticket
meta_description: What is free in Palermo and Monreale, which doors need a ticket (the cloister, the Salinas museum, Palazzo Riso), and how to reach Monreale by bus.

featured_image.alt: The cloister garden of Monreale with its rows of paired columns and a tower of the cathedral behind

content_html:
[place attraction="monreale-cathedral" city="palermo"]

The story told at Monreale is that William II, the Norman king of Sicily, fell asleep under a carob tree while hunting on the hill above Palermo. The Virgin appeared to him and said that a treasure lay under the tree, and that he was to build her a church with it. The likelier reason is less pious. The archbishop of Palermo was powerful and was rebuilding his own cathedral, and the king wanted a great church that answered to him.

He began in 1174, when he was about twenty, and spent without limit. Within a few years the walls carried more than six thousand square metres of gold mosaic. William died in 1189 at thirty-six and is buried there. Both cathedrals survive, eight kilometres apart, and since 2015 both have been on the UNESCO list with seven other Arab-Norman monuments. For a visitor the rivalry has a practical side: a good deal here is free, and a ticket desk tends to sit just past the free part.

Monreale: the church and the cloister are two visits

The cathedral

The whole interior is mosaic on a gold ground: the Old Testament along the nave, the life of Christ in the aisles and, in the apse, a figure of Christ so large that it holds the building together. The bronze doors of the west front are signed by Bonanno of Pisa and dated 1186.

For many years you walked in for nothing and paid only for extras such as the roof terraces. More recently visitors have been asked to pay for the visit itself. Plan on a ticket. The church closes to visitors in the middle of the day and during services, and you need covered shoulders and knees.

The apse of Monreale Cathedral, with the Pantocrator that looks down the whole nave. Photo: Mboesch, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The cloister

The cloister belonged to the abbey beside the cathedral. It has a separate door on the square, a separate ticket and its own hours. Its arcades rest on 228 small columns set in pairs, many of them inlaid with strips of mosaic, and no two capitals are the same: Bible scenes, animals, knights, and the king offering his church. In one corner a fountain stands in its own little court, its shaft carved like the trunk of a palm.

It takes half an hour and is the quietest place on the hill. If you care for sculpture, pay for it. If you came for the gold, the church is enough.

One of the capitals of the cloister. No two are the same. Photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

How to get up to Monreale

Monreale sits on a hillside south-west of the city. City bus 389 has long run there from Piazza Indipendenza, behind the Norman Palace. It is not frequent and it fills, and the ride takes half an hour or more in traffic. Buy the bus ticket at a tobacconist or kiosk before you board. A regional coach also runs from near the central station, and a taxi is quick if you agree the fare first.

Go up in the morning, because of the midday closing, and allow half a day in all. On Sundays and holidays the cloister has often closed early.

What is free in Palermo

  • Palermo Cathedral. The nave is free. The tombs of the Norman kings and of the emperor Frederick II, the treasury, the crypt and the walk on the roof have a ticket.
  • The Quattro Canti, the crossroads of the old city, built from 1608 with four curved fronts of statues and fountains.
  • Piazza Pretoria, round the corner, with its large fountain of marble nudes, made in Florence in the sixteenth century.
  • The markets of Ballarò and the Capo, which are at their best before noon.
  • The outsides: the Norman Palace, the red domes of San Giovanni degli Eremiti, the Teatro Massimo.

Many small churches, the Martorana among them, ask for a modest fee at the door.

What needs a ticket

  • The Palatine Chapel, inside the Norman Palace: the royal chapel of the 1130s and 1140s, with mosaics and a carved and painted wooden ceiling made by Arab craftsmen. It is the most expensive ticket in the city and the one to buy. The partner does not sell it.
  • The Salinas archaeological museum, in a former convent near the Teatro Massimo, round two cloisters. Its treasure is the set of carved reliefs from the Greek temples of Selinunte, on the south coast: Perseus cutting off the head of Medusa, Actaeon torn by his dogs. It also keeps the Palermo Stone, a fragment of an Egyptian list of kings. Allow an hour and a half. Not every floor has been open in recent years.
  • Palazzo Riso, on the old main street between the cathedral and the Quattro Canti. An eighteenth-century palace, bombed in 1943 and restored, it is now the regional museum of contemporary art. What you see depends on the exhibition, so look up what is on.

A room of the Salinas museum, with some of the smaller reliefs from Selinunte. Photo: Fabrizio Garrisi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Palazzo Belmonte Riso on the old main street, now the museum of contemporary art. Photo: Matthias Süßen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Monreale ticket is for the cloister only. It does not open the cathedral.
  • The Salinas and Palazzo Riso tickets are plain entry.
  • All three add a downloadable audio guide app about Sicily, in English and Italian, sent by separate email. It is a general companion, so do not expect a room-by-room commentary.
  • You show the voucher at the ticket office and go in at the next free time. It is not a way past a queue. Under-18s and young EU citizens have their own categories: pick the right one and bring an identity document.
  • The UNESCO audio tour is a two-hour walk in the partner's app, from Porta Nuova past the Norman Palace to Piazza Pretoria, the Martorana and the seafront. It includes no entry tickets.
  • The Segesta ticket is for a Greek temple and theatre more than an hour's drive from Palermo. The "shuttle" in its title runs inside the park, from the entrance up to the theatre. It is not transport from the city.

These are the tickets and the audio tour our partner sells in and around Palermo, with today's prices:

[partner city="palermo" match="monreale,salinas,riso,unesco" limit="5"]

A day in order

Take the bus to Monreale by nine and be back in town by one. Eat at a market. Give the hot hours to the Salinas museum, which is cool and never crowded. Then walk the old main street: Palazzo Riso, the Quattro Canti, Piazza Pretoria, and the cathedral before it closes. Current hours are on our pages for Monreale Cathedral and the Salinas museum.

From here

West of the centre stands the Zisa, a Norman summer palace built by Arab masons, on the same UNESCO list. The third great Norman cathedral, at Cefalù, is about an hour along the coast by train, with a beach below it. See the pages for Palermo Cathedral and the rest of Palermo, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Berthold Werner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is Monreale Cathedral free to enter?
faqs.a: It was for many years. More recently visitors have been asked to pay for the visit, with the roof terraces as an extra, so plan on a ticket. The cloister next door has always had a separate one.

faqs.q: Is the cloister of Monreale worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like sculpture: 228 paired columns, many inlaid with mosaic, each with a different carved capital, and a corner fountain. It takes about half an hour and is far quieter than the church.

faqs.q: How do you get from Palermo to Monreale?
faqs.a: By city bus from Piazza Indipendenza, behind the Norman Palace, by regional coach from near the central station, or by taxi. Go in the morning, because the cathedral closes to visitors in the middle of the day.

faqs.q: Is Palermo Cathedral free?
faqs.a: The nave is free. The royal tombs, the treasury, the crypt and the roof walk need a ticket.

faqs.q: What is in the Salinas museum in Palermo?
faqs.a: Sicily's main archaeological collection, in a former convent: above all the carved temple reliefs from Selinunte, and the Palermo Stone, a fragment of an Egyptian list of kings.

title: Palma Cathedral and the Almudaina palace: which ticket to buy, and what the audio tours include
subtitle: Two buildings side by side above the sea, with two owners, two tickets and several audio products around them.
excerpt: What the ticket for Palma Cathedral covers and what it leaves out, what you see in the Almudaina palace next door, whether to buy one or both, and what each of the partner's tickets and audio tours really includes.
longtail_phrases: which ticket to buy for Palma Cathedral
is the Almudaina palace worth visiting
is Palma Cathedral free to enter
what did Gaudí do in Palma Cathedral
how long do you need for Palma Cathedral
meta_title: Palma Cathedral and the Almudaina: which ticket
meta_description: What the Palma Cathedral ticket covers, what is in the Almudaina palace next door, one or both, and what the audio tours include and leave out.

featured_image.alt: The long buttressed side of Palma Cathedral above the old sea wall, seen across the lake of the Parc de la Mar

content_html:
[place attraction="palma-cathedral" city="palma"]

In September 1229 James I of Aragon, who was twenty-one, sailed from the Catalan coast with a fleet to take Mallorca from its Moorish rulers. Tradition says a storm caught the ships on the crossing, and the king vowed to build a church to the Virgin if he came through. The city fell on the last day of the year. Work on the church began on the site of the main mosque, and went on, with long pauses, for nearly four centuries.

The king and his successors lived next door, in the castle of the Moorish governors, the Almudaina. The two buildings still stand wall to wall above the old shoreline, and from the sea they look like one monument. They are not. The cathedral belongs to the Church and the palace to the Spanish crown. Each has its own door, its own hours and its own ticket, and there is no joint one. So the question is which to buy, and what the tickets and audio tours sold around them really cover.

The palace in front, the cathedral behind: two doors, two owners, two tickets. Photo: Wolfgang Moroder, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The cathedral: what you see

The nave is 44 metres high, among the tallest in Gothic Europe, and stands on eight-sided pillars so slender that the space reads as a single hall. Above the altar, at the east end, is a rose window more than eleven metres across. In the morning the sun comes through it and scatters colour down the nave, which is why the first hours of the day are the ones to choose.

Two modern artists worked here. Antoni Gaudí spent ten years on the interior from 1904: he moved the choir stalls out of the middle of the nave, opened up the view to the altar, and hung over it a wide canopy of iron, lamps and cloth that was meant as a trial piece and never replaced. He left in 1914 after a quarrel. A century later the Mallorcan painter Miquel Barceló covered a chapel to the right of the altar with a skin of cracked clay, full of fish, loaves and fruit, finished in 2007.

The nave, with the canopy that Gaudí hung over the altar at the far end. Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What the cathedral ticket covers

  • Covered: the church itself. The partner's listing also names the Museum of Sacred Art as part of the ticket.
  • Not covered: the roof terraces. They are a separate ticket, offered in the warmer months, at set times, to small groups, up a long spiral stair. If you want them, book ahead.
  • Free: attending Mass. That is worship and not a visit, and you cannot walk round.

On Sundays the cathedral has generally been open for services only. Shoulders and knees should be covered, and luggage is not allowed in. Allow an hour.

The great rose window above the altar, best in the morning. Photo: Antonio De Lorenzo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5.

The Almudaina: what you see

The palace was a Moorish fortress, rebuilt in Gothic style from 1309 for James II of Mallorca. It is still an official residence of the King of Spain, who uses it for receptions in the summer. The route goes through the stone-arched halls of the ground floor, hung with tapestries, up to the royal apartments, and out to a courtyard with the chapel of St Anne and its Romanesque doorway. From the terrace you look over the harbour.

It takes about three quarters of an hour and is much quieter than the cathedral. It is usually shut on Mondays and can close without warning for official events. Like other royal sites in Spain it has free hours on certain afternoons for some visitors. If you qualify and your day is flexible, you need no paid ticket, but expect a line.

The stone arches of the great hall of the Almudaina. Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

Which ticket

  • Only one: the cathedral. There is nothing else like it on the island.
  • Both: the natural choice for a morning. The doors are a minute apart, and the pair takes two hours. Do the cathedral first, for the light, and the palace after.
  • Neither: the outside is free and very good. Walk the sea wall and the Parc de la Mar, where the cathedral is reflected in a lake, then the gardens of S'Hort del Rei under the palace.
  • The terraces: only if stairs are no trouble and you have booked.

What the partner's tickets and audio tours include

  • Cathedral ticket with an audio guide and a city walk. The entry ticket, plus commentary in the partner's app: first inside the cathedral, then a walk of about two hours past the Parc de la Mar, the Arab Baths, the church of Sant Francesc, the town hall square and the old exchange, ending outside the Almudaina. Entry to the palace and the baths is not included, and the terraces are excluded.
  • The same audio tour without a ticket. The title says so. It is for people who already hold a cathedral ticket or want only the walk. Check which of the two you are putting in the basket.
  • Almudaina entry with a "digital royal guide". Entry at a set time. The guide is a PDF to read on your phone, not an audio guide.
  • The Jewish quarter audio tour. One hour in the lanes east of the cathedral. No entries.
  • The trivia audio tour. A longer old town walk with quiz questions on the way. No entries.

All the audio runs in the partner's app on your own phone. Download it before you leave the hotel and bring earphones.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for the cathedral, the palace and the old town, with today's prices:

[partner city="palma" match="cathedral,almudaina,jewish,trivia" limit="5"]

Practical notes

The visitor door of the cathedral changes with the season, between the sea side and the square, and your ticket says which. When cruise ships are in port the church is fullest from mid-morning to early afternoon, so go at opening or late. Hours for both buildings change through the year: see our pages for Palma Cathedral and the Royal Palace of La Almudaina.

From here

The Arab Baths, one small domed room in a garden, are five minutes east and charge a little at the gate. Down by the harbour, the old exchange is a fifteenth-century merchants' hall with twisted columns, free when an exhibition is on. On a wooded hill three kilometres west stands Bellver Castle, a round Gothic castle with the best view of the bay. See what else there is in Palma, or open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Which ticket should you buy for Palma Cathedral?
faqs.a: The standard cathedral ticket is enough for most visitors. The roof terraces are a separate ticket in the warmer months, and the Almudaina palace next door has its own ticket too.

faqs.q: Is the Almudaina palace worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have a spare hour after the cathedral. It is a medieval royal palace with stone halls, tapestries and a harbour view, and it is much quieter. With time for only one, choose the cathedral.

faqs.q: Is Palma Cathedral free to enter?
faqs.a: Not for a visit. Tourists pay for a ticket. Attending Mass is free, but you cannot walk round the church during a service.

faqs.q: What did Gaudí do in Palma Cathedral?
faqs.a: Between 1904 and 1914 he moved the choir stalls out of the middle of the nave, opened the view to the altar and hung a large canopy over it. He left before the work was finished.

faqs.q: How long do you need for Palma Cathedral?
faqs.a: About an hour for the cathedral. With the Almudaina palace next door, allow two hours for the pair.

title: Loro Parque or Siam Park in Tenerife: which one to choose, the combined ticket, and getting there
subtitle: An animal park in the cloudy north, a water park in the sunny south, one owner and a motorway between them.

featured_image.alt: A pink pavilion with Moorish arches, parrot statues, a small pool and a lawn among palm trees at Loro Parque in Tenerife

content_html:
[place attraction="loro-parque" city="puerto-de-la-cruz"]

On 17 December 1972 a German businessman, Wolfgang Kiessling, opened a small park in Puerto de la Cruz, on the north coast of Tenerife. It had 150 parrots and a parrot show. "Loro" is the Spanish word for parrot. At that time the north was where visitors to the island stayed, in a green valley under the peak of Teide.

Over the next decades tourism moved to the dry, sunny south, and the park stayed where it was and grew: penguins, gorillas, an aquarium, dolphins, orcas, and the largest collection of parrot species in the world. In 2008 the same family opened a second park in the south, at Costa Adeje, a water park in Thai style called Siam Park. So there are two parks with one owner at opposite ends of the island, sold separately and together. A family with a week has to decide: one, the other, or both.

What each park is

Loro Parque

A zoo with shows, laid out as a tropical garden. You walk from parrots to gorillas to an indoor penguin house where snow falls on a rock island, through a tunnel under sharks, and between times you sit in the arenas where sea lions, dolphins, orcas and parrots perform at fixed hours. The day is built round that timetable. Allow five to six hours.

The park keeps orcas and dolphins and stages shows with them. Some visitors prefer not to support that. It is your decision, and it is better made before buying.

King penguins in the indoor penguin house at Loro Parque. Photo: AnatolyPm, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Siam Park

A water park with heated water. The best-known ride is the Tower of Power, a near-vertical slide 28 metres high that ends in a clear tube through a tank of fish. There are raft rides for groups, a slow river, a wave pool with a sand beach, and a children's area with small slides. People stay all day.

Siam Park from the air, with the wave pool and its beach in the middle. Photo: Wouter Hagens, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which one for whom

  • Small children: Loro Parque. Siam Park has height limits on its rides (the partner's listing gives 1.10, 1.25 and 1.40 metres), and a child below the first is kept to the children's area, the river and the edge of the pool.
  • Teenagers: Siam Park, without much discussion.
  • Three generations together: Loro Parque, which asks nothing of you but walking and has shade and seats.
  • A cloudy day: Loro Parque. The north coast is often under cloud, and much of the park is indoors or under trees.
  • A winter visit: Siam Park is open and the water is warm, but the air may not be. Pick your sunniest day. In winter single rides also close for maintenance, sometimes for weeks: the listing says which.
  • Glasses: the listing warns that they may not be worn on some slides.

The combined ticket

It is one entry to each park. The listing says that after the first visit you have fifteen days for the second. Confirm that when you book. Using both on the same day is allowed and makes no sense, since each park fills a day and they are over an hour apart.

It is worth buying only if you would visit both in any case, so compare it with the two single tickets. It does not include transport between the parks, fast-track access to the slides, lockers and towels at Siam Park, food or parking.

Getting to Loro Parque

From the south (Los Cristianos, Playa de las Américas, Costa Adeje) the motorway goes round the east of the island by way of Santa Cruz. It is about a hundred kilometres, and an hour and a quarter to an hour and a half each way. You can hire a car, and pay for the car park, which is limited. You can take a ticket that includes a coach: on the partner's listing it leaves from a meeting point in Playa de las Américas, takes ninety minutes each way and starts back from the park at 16:30. Or you can use the public express bus between the southern resorts and Puerto de la Cruz, which runs a few times a day.

From Puerto de la Cruz a free road train runs to the park from Plaza de los Reyes Católicos about every twenty minutes, according to the listing. On foot it is twenty minutes along the seafront.

From Santa Cruz and La Laguna there are frequent buses to Puerto de la Cruz.

Puerto de la Cruz, the town of Loro Parque, on the green north coast under Teide. Photo: Mrgnr0, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Getting to Siam Park

The park lies beside the southern motorway at Costa Adeje. From much of Playa de las Américas you can walk there, and the park has run free buses from Los Cristianos, Las Américas and Costa Adeje: stops and times are on the listing. From the north it is the same motorway in reverse, so leave early.

You may not bring in your own food or drink. Take a towel, or rent one, and expect to pay for a locker.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Loro Parque and Siam Park, combined entry, as above.
  • Siam Park entry includes sun loungers, floats, life jackets, changing rooms and showers. Fast-track access, lockers and towels are extra.
  • Loro Parque entry with transport is the coach from the south described above, with the park ticket.
  • Jungle Park entry is a different, smaller animal park in the hills above Los Cristianos, known for its birds of prey flying free over the audience. The listing mentions a free shuttle from the resorts. It is a half-day choice for a family in the south that does not want to cross the island.

The plain Loro Parque ticket, without transport, is on our page for Loro Parque.

A sun conure at Loro Parque. The park began in 1972 with parrots and nothing else. Photo: H. Zell, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

From here

Puerto de la Cruz is worth the rest of the day if you came north by car: the seawater pools of Lago Martiánez, designed by César Manrique, the black sand of Playa Jardín beside the park, and a botanical garden founded in 1788. Inland, the road climbs through La Orotava to Teide National Park. Our page for Siam Park has its current hours, and the trip planner for Spain fits the island into a longer route.

Cover photo: Tuxyso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is Loro Parque or Siam Park better?
faqs.a: They are different things. Loro Parque is a zoo with shows and suits small children, mixed ages and cloudy days. Siam Park is a water park and suits teenagers and adults who want slides, on a sunny day.

faqs.q: Can you do Loro Parque and Siam Park in one day?
faqs.a: It is allowed but not sensible. Each park fills a day, and they are at opposite ends of the island, over an hour apart. The combined ticket lets you visit them on different days.

faqs.q: How do you get to Loro Parque from Costa Adeje?
faqs.a: By hire car on the motorway by way of Santa Cruz, in about an hour and a quarter to an hour and a half. Otherwise book a ticket that includes a coach from the south, or take the public express bus to Puerto de la Cruz.

faqs.q: Is Siam Park suitable for small children?
faqs.a: Partly. The rides have height limits starting at 1.10 metres, so smaller children are kept to the children's area, the slow river and the edge of the wave pool. Loro Parque is the easier day with toddlers.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Loro Parque?
faqs.a: Five to six hours, because the day is built round the timetable of the shows. With travel from the south of the island it takes the whole day.
